answer:
Let the slide-to-lens distance be \(u\), the lens-to-screen distance be \(v\), and the fixed slide-screen separation be  
\[
L=u+v=90\text{ cm}.
\]
For a sharp real image,
\[
\frac1f=\frac1u+\frac1v
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
uv=fL.
\]
The two lens positions correspond to the two roots of
\[
u^2-Lu+fL=0.
\]
Their separation is
\[
d=\sqrt{L^2-4fL}.
\]
Given \(d=30\text{ cm}\),
\[
f=\frac{L^2-d^2}{4L}
=\frac{90^2-30^2}{4(90)}
=\frac{8100-900}{360}=20\text{ cm}.
\]

The two object distances are
\[
u=\frac{L\pm d}{2}=\frac{90\pm30}{2}=30\text{ cm},\ 60\text{ cm}.
\]
Thus the two conjugate pairs are:
\[
(u,v)=(30,60)\text{ cm}
\]
or
\[
(u,v)=(60,30)\text{ cm}.
\]

Using the usual sign convention for a real inverted image,
\[
m=-\frac{v}{u},
\]
so
\[
m_1=-\frac{60}{30}=-2,
\qquad
m_2=-\frac{30}{60}=-\frac12.
\]
That is, one position gives a twice-size inverted image, and the other gives a half-size inverted image.

Check:
\[
\frac1{30}+\frac1{60}
=\frac{2}{60}+\frac1{60}
=\frac3{60}
=\frac1{20},
\]
and
\[
\frac1{60}+\frac1{30}
=\frac1{20},
\]
so in both cases \(f=20\text{ cm}\).

Both magnifications are negative under the standard convention because both real images are inverted. The signs alone do not distinguish the two lens positions; they only indicate inversion. The magnitudes, \(2\) and \(1/2\), distinguish the positions: the image is magnified when the slide is closer to the lens \((u=30\text{ cm})\), and reduced when it is farther \((u=60\text{ cm})\).

\[
\boxed{f=20\text{ cm},\qquad m=-2\ \text{or}\ -\frac12}
\]

with the two positions having \((u,v)=(30,60)\text{ cm}\) and \((60,30)\text{ cm}\).
